content_voiceover: This diagram lays out the classic coagulation cascade, and it's worth reviewing since it's the framework for interpreting every screening test we've discussed. On the left is the intrinsic pathway, beginning with factor twelve, the Hageman factor, which is activated by contact with negatively charged surfaces and works with prekallikrein and high molecular weight kininogen. Activated factor twelve activates factor eleven, which activates factor nine, and factor nine, together with its cofactor factor eight and calcium on a phospholipid surface, activates factor ten. On the right is the extrinsic pathway, triggered by tissue injury: tissue factor is exposed and binds factor seven, and this tissue factor-factor seven-a complex also activates factor ten. Both pathways converge on factor ten, entering the common pathway. Activated factor ten, with cofactor factor five, calcium, and phospholipid, converts prothrombin, factor two, into thrombin, factor two-a. Thrombin then cleaves fibrinogen into fibrin, and factor thirteen, activated by thrombin, cross-links the fibrin strands into a stable clot. Remember that the PT tests the extrinsic and common pathways, so it's sensitive to factor seven, while the aPTT tests the intrinsic and common pathways, sensitive to factors twelve, eleven, nine, and eight.
keypoints: Intrinsic pathway: factor XII to XI to IX, with factor VIII as cofactor, activating factor X
Extrinsic pathway: tissue factor binds factor VII, activating factor X
Both pathways converge at factor X, the start of the common pathway
Common pathway: factor Xa with factor V converts prothrombin to thrombin
Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and factor XIII cross-links the clot
keypoint_voiceover: Recall the cascade: intrinsic pathway factors twelve, eleven, nine, and eight feed into factor ten; extrinsic pathway tissue factor and factor seven also feed into factor ten; factor ten and five generate thrombin from prothrombin, and thrombin converts fibrinogen to cross-linked fibrin via factor thirteen.
